Keep a left boundary and a dictionary of the most recent position of each character. When the next character has already appeared inside the window, both copies cannot stay. Moving `left` just beyond the earlier copy removes the conflict in one jump. A remembered occurrence outside the window is harmless, so it must never pull `left` backward.

After this repair, the current window is the longest distinct-character substring ending here. Compare its length with `best`, then continue. Notice that the dictionary can remember old positions without deleting them: the left boundary tells us which positions still matter. This separates historical information from the active window and makes the algorithm linear.

steps: For `abcabcbb`, start with `left=0`, `best=0`, and an empty last-position dictionary.
Reading `a`, `b`, `c` at positions 0, 1, 2 grows the distinct window `abc` to length 3.
At position 3, `a` last appeared at 0 inside the window. Move `left` to 1; `bca` is valid and still length 3.
The following `b` and `c` move `left` to 2 and then 3. No window becomes longer than 3.
At position 6, `b` previously occurred at 4, so `left` jumps to 5. The final `b` moves `left` to 7.
The longest recorded length is 3, returned after every `right` endpoint has been considered.

concept.question: How far can a strip of letters grow before a repeat forces it to shrink?
intuition: Checking every possible continuous section repeats the same character comparisons. A section that was valid a moment ago only needs one new question when we add the next letter: does this new letter already appear inside it?

Imagine a movable frame over the string. Extend its far edge one character at a time. When the new character repeats one inside the frame, move the near edge just past that earlier occurrence. Remember the widest valid frame ever seen.
concept.observation: The start only moves forward. An earlier copy outside the frame does not invalidate the current frame.
approach: Extend the framed section by one character.
If that character already appears inside, move the start just past its previous occurrence.
Remember the greatest valid length after each extension.
concept.correctness: For each ending position, moving just beyond the latest conflicting character gives the earliest possible valid start. Any earlier start would include a duplicate. Thus the frame is the longest valid section ending there. Taking the maximum over all endings gives the overall longest substring.

complexity.explanation: Scan each character once and remember its latest position. The start never moves backward. Time grows with the string length; memory grows with the number of distinct characters encountered.

pitfalls: A substring must be continuous; skipping characters changes the problem.
Do not move the start backward.
Spaces and punctuation count as characters.
